title: Prime Factor Trees

els.text: Use a factor tree to write a number as a product of primes, then in index form.

•  Draw a factor tree, circling every prime
•  Write a product of primes in index form, such as $2^2 \times 3$

A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.

The primes up to 20 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19.

1 is not a prime number.
How to draw a factor tree

Split it into two numbers
(not using 1)
Ask it again for each new number

els.text: Index form is a short way to write the same number multiplied by itself again and again.
The small raised number is the index. It counts how many times the number is written.

items.title: Who is right about $7^{3}$?
answer: Leo is right: $7^{3}$ means three 7s multiplied together, $7 \times 7 \times 7 = 343$.

options.reasoning: Multiplies the 7 by the index: $7 \times 3 = 21$. The index counts the 7s.
$7 \times 3 = 21$ is not $343$: the index is a count, not a times.

question: Who is right?
explanation: The small 3 says the 7 is written three times.

misconception.label: Reads the index as a multiplier instead of a count of repeats

items.title: Is the tree for $48$ finished?
answer: Ruby is right: $6$ and $8$ are not prime. $6 = 2 \times 3$ and $8 = 2 \times 4$, so keep splitting.

els.text:
•  Is it prime? Circle it. If not, split it into two numbers and ask again.
•  A factor tree ends when every branch ends in a circled prime.
•  Index form counts the repeats: $2 \times 2 \times 3 = 2^2 \times 3$.

summary: One lesson for a weak group after LCM and HCF: draw factor trees to write a number as a product of primes, then in index form. Harry draws the trees; the deck has the method as a flow chart, lots of whiteboard and book practice with answers only, and a short index-form section. No calculators.
